title: Is anybody out there?
text: On a clear night, far from the lights of a city, you can see thousands of stars with the naked eye. Each of them is a sun, and we now know that many of them have planets travelling around them. Faced with such enormous numbers, it is hard not to ask one of the oldest questions of all: are we alone in the universe? For centuries, this was a question for philosophers and science fiction writers. Today, it is one that scientists are seriously trying to answer.

The search begins surprisingly close to home. For a long time, Mars was considered the most promising place to look, and several robotic rovers have explored its surface. They have found clear evidence that rivers and lakes once existed there, billions of years ago, when the planet was warmer and wetter. If life ever appeared on Mars, scientists hope to find traces of it in ancient rocks, and samples are already being collected for that purpose.

More recently, however, attention has shifted to some unexpected places: the icy moons of Jupiter and Saturn. Europa, one of the moons of Jupiter, is covered by a thick shell of ice, but beneath it there is thought to be a huge ocean of liquid water. Enceladus, a small moon of Saturn, is even more intriguing. In 2005, the Cassini spacecraft observed giant jets of water shooting out of cracks near its south pole. On Earth, wherever there is liquid water, there is life, so these moons have become top targets for future missions.

Beyond our solar system, the possibilities multiply. Since the first planets orbiting other stars were confirmed in the nineteen nineties, astronomers have discovered more than five thousand of them. Some are giant balls of gas, but others are rocky worlds of a similar size to Earth, orbiting at a distance from their star where water could exist as a liquid. New telescopes are now able to study the atmospheres of a few of these planets, looking for gases that might be produced by living things.

Of course, finding bacteria on a distant moon would be very different from meeting intelligent beings. Since 1960, some researchers have been listening for radio signals from other civilisations, so far without success. This silence has led to a famous puzzle, known as the Fermi paradox. If the universe is so vast and so old, and life is not unusual, then where is everybody?

There are many possible answers. Perhaps intelligent life is extremely rare. Perhaps civilisations exist but are too far away, or communicate in ways we do not understand. Some scientists even suggest that we simply have not been searching for long enough, since our technology has existed for only a tiny fraction of the history of the universe.

Whatever the truth, the search itself is changing the way we see our own planet. Every discovery reminds us how special the conditions on Earth are. And if one day we do receive a message from the stars, it will probably be the most important news in human history.

parts.help: Use the word in capitals at the end of each gap to form a word that fits.
